“weep and howl” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, James 5:1 and — as two clauses rather than one phrase — Joel 1:5, so James is effectively the only place the collocation stands as a unit. But James 5:1 is a prophetic summons addressed to the guilty in advance of judgment — ‘Go to now, ye rich men, weep and howl for your miseries that shall come upon you’ — and 3 Nephi 10:8 describes the spared grieving after judgment for kindred and friends already dead. The Book of Mormon has also used ‘lamenting and howling’ at 10:2 in the same sense, which suggests a narrator's own idiom for mass grief rather than a borrowing.

“remnant of Joseph” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and Amos 5:15's remnant is a remnant spared from a national judgment on condition of doing justice — which is very close to what 3 Nephi 10:12-17 is about, so the case deserves stating before it is declined. It is declined on distribution. The Book of Mormon's phrase is ‘a remnant of the seed of Joseph’, and “remnant of the seed” occurs in no KJV verse at all while occurring thirteen times in the Book of Mormon (1 Nephi 13:38-39, 3 Nephi 5:23-24, Alma 46:23-27, Ether 13:6-10, Mormon 5:24 and here). It is one of the book's own standing formulae, built on its own covenant argument about Joseph's coat, and the intervening ‘of the seed’ is exactly what separates it from Amos. A formula the Book of Mormon uses thirteen times cannot be sourced to a KJV verse it does not match.

Ezekiel 20:17 is God declining to destroy Israel in the wilderness — ‘neither did I make an end of them’ — where ‘make an end of’ takes a people as its object and means annihilate. Mormon's ‘I make an end of my sayings’ takes a discourse as its object and means stop talking; it is his standing colophon formula, used at the close of books and sections throughout. Two senses of one English phrasal verb, and no other contact.
